\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{कीटः} (kīṭaḥ)}{कीटः (kīṭaḥ)}]{\sk{कीटः} (kīṭaḥ) — an insect}

\label{lesson:SA-C253-kitah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for jasmine, then the Sanskrit for holy basil.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कीटः}}
\textbf{\sk{कीटः}} — \emph{kīṭaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}an insect\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kīṭa} is an insect or worm, already in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (CDIAL 3193). MW gives no derivation, so its origin is uncertain. It lives on as Hindi \emph{kīṛā}, \textquotedblleft{}insect, worm\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{लूता} (lūtā)}{लूता (lūtā)}]{\sk{लूता} (lūtā) — a spider}

\label{lesson:SA-C253-luta}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for holy basil, then the Sanskrit for an insect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{लूता}}
\textbf{\sk{लूता}} — \emph{lūtā} — \textquotedblleft{}a spider\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{lūtā} is a spider in Manu (CDIAL 11093). Neither MW nor CDIAL derives it, so its origin is uncertain. It also named a skin disease said to come from spiders, and Hindi \emph{lūtā} keeps that sense.
\end{cousinweb}

\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{वृश्चिकः} (vṛścikaḥ)}{वृश्चिकः (vṛścikaḥ)}]{\sk{वृश्चिकः} (vṛścikaḥ) — a scorpion}

\label{lesson:SA-C253-vrscikah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for an insect, then the Sanskrit for a spider.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वृश्चिकः}}
\textbf{\sk{वृश्चिकः}} — \emph{vṛścikaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a scorpion\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vṛścika} is a Rigvedic word for the scorpion (CDIAL 12081), probably built on the root √vraśc, \textquotedblleft{}to cut, tear\textquotedblright{}, though CDIAL marks that with a question mark. It is also the sign Scorpio, and Hindi \emph{bīchā} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{गोधा} (godhā)}{गोधा (godhā)}]{\sk{गोधा} (godhā) — a lizard}

\label{lesson:SA-C253-godha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a spider, then the Sanskrit for a scorpion.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{गोधा}}
\textbf{\sk{गोधा}} — \emph{godhā} — \textquotedblleft{}a lizard\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{godhā} is a big lizard, the monitor, in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā. CDIAL 4286 thinks it probably came from Dravidian and was reshaped by folk etymology to look like \emph{go}, \textquotedblleft{}cow\textquotedblright{}, and it points to Mayrhofer for an Indo-European account, so the question is not settled. It lives on as Hindi \emph{goh}, \textquotedblleft{}iguana\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{नक्रः} (nakraḥ)}{नक्रः (nakraḥ)}]{\sk{नक्रः} (nakraḥ) — a crocodile}

\label{lesson:SA-C253-nakrah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a scorpion, then the Sanskrit for a lizard.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{नक्रः}}
\textbf{\sk{नक्रः}} — \emph{nakraḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a crocodile\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nakra} is a crocodile or alligator, and also the sign Scorpio (MW). MW reports a grammarians' analysis into \emph{na} and \emph{kra}, but gives no sure derivation, so its origin is uncertain.
\end{cousinweb}
